note:
Your report (8 Oct), after #113: it gained many small lakes and islands, but the really small ones still disappear at low zooms, and it isn't consistent across zooms. Northern Quebec at z6.6 shows many more lakes than at z6.4.

What I found (not yet measured):
- The water is drawn as raster tiles holding each pixel's exact share of water (coverage), 512 px a tile shown at 256 CSS px. MapLibre switches tile level at each half zoom.
  - At z6.4 it draws the z7 tiles enlarged 1.32×: a 50 m lake is a few percent of one pixel there, so it shows as a few percent of tint. That's barely visible on the dark land.
  - At z6.6 it draws the z8 tiles shrunk 0.76×, without mipmaps. Its linear sampling picks texels where small lakes have higher coverage, so they show stronger, sparkly but visible.
  - So the jump at each half zoom is partly the filtering, and the fade at z6.4 is the exact-coverage design itself: a true downsample of full detail makes tiny lakes faint.
- This conflicts with plan.md's principle ("Zoomed out, nothing small leaves the map: every road… and every island and lake too"). That text still describes the old dots, so the docs are out of date too.

Your call: what should a lake much smaller than a pixel look like zoomed out?
- (a) exactly its share of the pixel (true downsampling: faint), made consistent across zooms;
- (b) always visible: a floor on its contrast, so every lake and island stays a visible speck at every zoom, its size still true where it's bigger than a pixel.

My recommendation: (b), matching the plan's principle and what you're asking for. Either way, the jump between tile levels gets fixed and measured with #113's harness on dense lake regions at fractional zooms.
text: Water: small lakes and islands still fade out zoomed out, and differ from one zoom to the next (northern Quebec: z6.4 shows far fewer lakes than z6.6)
